en.title: What is Threads, and should a small brand be on it?
en.seoTitle: What is Threads? Should a small brand be on it
en.description: How Threads differs from Facebook and Instagram, which businesses it suits, which should wait, and what to do in your first two weeks if you try it.
en.excerpt: Lately everyone seems to say “just ask on Threads”. If you sell something or run a brand and you’re wondering whether to open yet another channel, this post helps you decide in ten minutes.
en.body:
What Threads is, in plain words

Threads is Meta’s social network, from the same family as Facebook and Instagram. You usually sign in with your Instagram account, so you don’t have to build a profile from scratch.

The big difference: Threads is about words and conversation. Each post can be up to 500 characters, with photos or video if you like, but what brings a post to life is the replies underneath. People go to Threads to ask, to share stories, and to argue (gently) about which café is best, which lipstick lasts, which book is worth reading.

How it differs from Facebook and Instagram

Three differences matter if you run a brand:

  • Strangers see your posts. The “For you” feed shows posts from accounts people don’t follow yet. A new account with few followers can still get a lot of readers if a post makes people want to reply.
  • A conversational voice beats an ad voice. Posts that read like a press release get scrolled past. Posts that sound like a real person telling a story or asking a question get read.
  • Replies matter as much as posts. On Facebook, comments are an afterthought. On Threads, a reply is often where people first discover your brand.

Which businesses suit Threads

Threads works best for things people ask each other about before they buy:

  • Food and drink: restaurants, bakeries, cafés, delivery.
  • Beauty: cosmetics, skincare, spas, salons.
  • Books, courses, study supplies.
  • Local fashion brands and accessories.
  • Services that need trust: clinics, home repair, travel, software for small businesses.

What they have in common: customers like hearing about real experiences from other people. If your product gets questions like “has anyone tried this?”, you should be on Threads.

When it’s not worth it yet

To save you some effort:

  • You only want to post product photos with prices and wait for orders. Facebook and marketplaces still do that better.
  • Nobody will read and answer replies. On Threads, an unanswered reply section wastes the post.
  • Your product sells on looks alone, like high-end furniture. Threads can still work, but Instagram usually works better.

If you try it, what to do in the first two weeks

  1. Make your profile clear. Your logo as the profile photo, a one-line bio saying what you sell and where, and a single link.
  2. One post a day. It doesn’t need to be long. A real question, a small moment from the shop, a tip for using your product.
  3. Answer every reply in the first few hours. That’s when the post is travelling furthest.
  4. Find posts asking about exactly what you sell and reply from your brand account. Help first, mention yourself second.
  5. Review at the end of each week: which posts got the most replies? Do a few more like those next week.

For example, a bánh mì shop in District 3 could open with: “Honest question: for breakfast bánh mì, do you want a lot of pâté or just a little? We can’t agree on this in the shop.” It sells nothing, but everyone who reads it has an opinion.

In short

Threads won’t replace Facebook or Instagram. It’s where a brand talks with customers, and where strangers discover you through those conversations. If people in your industry ask each other before they buy, give it two serious weeks and then decide.

en.title: How to grow engagement on Threads for a small shop: 7 things to do now
en.seoTitle: How to grow engagement on Threads for a small shop: 7 things to do now
en.description: Seven concrete ways to get more readers and replies on a small shop’s Threads posts: how to open, when to post, replying to comments, joining the right discussions.
en.excerpt: Posting regularly but still getting a handful of likes? Usually it isn’t the product. It’s that the post hasn’t given readers a reason to stop. Here are seven things you can start this week.
en.body:
1. Open with a line people want to answer

The first line decides whether people scroll past or stop. Don’t open with your shop name or a slogan. Open with a real question, or an opinion that makes the reader want to say “not for me”.

Instead of “May Beauty launches a new lipstick line, gorgeous shades, great prices!”, try: “Do earthy lipstick shades actually work on tan skin, or do they only look good in photos? I tried 3 this week and the result surprised me.”

2. Tell small stories with real details

Anyone can write “busy day at the shop today”. Only your shop can write “at 7am a motorbike taxi driver stopped by and bought 12 bánh mì for his whole crew”. Specific details make a post sound like a real person talking, and real people get replies.

3. Reply to comments in the first hour or two

Right after you post is when it reaches the most people. Every reply you write makes the conversation longer, and posts with conversations travel further. Set a routine: post, come back after 30 minutes and again after 2 hours to reply.

Make your replies real replies, not just “thanks!”. Ask the person something back, or add a detail, and the conversation gets one more round.

4. Add exactly one topic

Threads lets you add one topic to each post. Pick the topic people interested in your product follow, like “Skincare”, “Saigon coffee” or “Book reviews”. One precise topic beats several generic ones.

5. Post regularly, at the same times

You don’t need five posts a day. One a day, steadily for a few weeks, beats posting a burst and then going quiet. Pick the times your customers scroll their phones: office workers at lunch and in the evening, students later at night. Try two time slots for two weeks and keep the one that gets more replies.

6. Join the discussions people are already having

Every day on Threads someone asks about exactly what you sell: “Any bánh mì place in District 1 with a really crunchy crust?”, “What sunscreen works for oily skin?”. That’s the best chance for strangers to discover you.

How to do it right:

  • Reply from your brand account and say who you are. People trust you more when you don’t hide it.
  • Help first, mention yourself second. Answer the actual question, suggest other good options if they fit, then mention your product.
  • Only join discussions that are genuinely relevant. Jumping into everything just annoys people.

7. Note which posts get replies

At the end of each week, look back at what you posted. Write down the three posts with the most replies and ask: how did it open, what was it about, what time did it go out? Next week, do a few more like those. After a month you’ll have your own “formula” for your shop, more reliable than any generic guide, this one included.

Things to avoid

  • Reposting your Facebook post word for word, with a dozen hashtags.
  • Putting a shop link in every post. Keep the link in your profile and mention it now and then.
  • Writing only in ad-speak. Out of ten posts, eight should be conversation and two can be about your product.

en.title: How to write Threads posts that strangers want to reply to
en.seoTitle: How to write Threads posts that strangers want to reply to
en.description: Why correct posts still get no replies, five kinds of posts that start conversations, a three-line formula, and before-and-after examples for small shops.
en.excerpt: You covered every point, the spelling is right, the photo looks great, and the post is still silent. Usually that’s because the post already said everything and left no room for the reader. This post shows you how to leave that room.
en.body:
Why a “correct” post still gets no replies

Look at a familiar post: “May Bakery’s wood-fired bánh mì: crunchy crust, soft inside, delivered in 30 minutes. Order now!”. Nothing is wrong with it. But after reading it, there’s nothing left to say. No question, nothing to agree or disagree with.

On Threads, posts travel further when people reply. So the writer’s job isn’t just to say enough. It’s to open a conversation.

Five kinds of posts that get replies

1. Pick one of two

Everyone has an opinion when asked to pick a side. “Vietnamese bánh mì or French baguette, which side are you on?” is far easier to answer than “What do you think of bánh mì?”.

2. Ask for a recommendation

“Looking for a book for a 2-hour bus ride home, something gentle, not too sad. Any suggestions?”. People like to help, especially when the question is specific enough that an answer pops into their head.

3. An opinion slightly against the crowd

“I don’t think expensive sunscreen is necessarily better than affordable ones, as long as you apply enough.” It doesn’t need to shock, it just needs a point of view. People who agree will say so, people who don’t will say why.

4. Tell half a story, then ask

“Yesterday a customer ordered 50 bánh mì at 5am for a wedding back in their hometown. We baked through the night and…”, then ask “What’s the most unexpected order you’ve ever had?”. The story pulls readers in, the closing question invites them to share their own.

5. An unfinished list

“Three quiet cafés in District 3 where I like to work: … Where else should I try?”. A list with gaps is an invitation for others to fill them.

The three-line formula

When you’re stuck, write exactly three lines:

  1. A real detail: something you just saw, did, or heard a customer say.
  2. Your take on that detail.
  3. A specific question for the reader.

For example, from a used bookshop: “A student came in this morning with a book they bought from us in 2019, an old bus ticket still tucked inside. I think the best part of used books is little traces like this. What’s the most surprising thing you’ve found in a used book?”

Four common mistakes

  • Opening with your brand name. Readers see an ad and scroll on. Move the brand name to the end, or let your profile do the talking.
  • Questions that are too broad. “What do you think?” is harder to answer than “Do you like a lot of pâté or just a little?”.
  • Writing too much. 500 characters is a limit, not a target. Posts of three or four sentences usually get read to the end.
  • Asking, then disappearing. If people reply and you never come back, next time they won’t reply either.

Before and after

Beauty shop. Before: “Authentic vitamin C serum, fades dark spots, brightens skin. DM us for advice.” After: “Vitamin C in the morning or at night? I switched back and forth for a month and the difference was real. When do you use yours?”

Bakery. Before: “Wood-fired bánh mì, 30-minute delivery in Districts 1 and 3.” After: “Day-old bánh mì goes chewy. How do you bring it back? We usually re-toast it for 3 minutes in the air fryer, but there must be a better way.”

The “after” posts don’t sell anything directly. But people who reply will tap through to see who the shop is, and that’s when they discover you.
